findings.body:
**Escaped JSON keys bypass every key regex and loosen the baseline unseen.**

`VALUE_RE` (`monotonicGuard.ts:147`) and `DIRECTION_KEY_RE`/`DIRECTION_RE`/`UNIT_KEY_RE`/`UNIT_RE` (`:173-178`) only match the literal spelling of each key. `JSON.parse` decodes escapes inside key names, so `"val\u0075e"` is the key `value`. When a key appears twice, the last occurrence wins.

How the bypass works on an existing `higher-is-better` baseline that has `"value": 80`:

```
-  "metric": "lines",
+  "metric": "lines", "val\u0075e": 50,
```

- Both sides have a VALUE_RE count of 0, and the context lines still show a value. So `valuesMoved === false` and `oldValue === newValue === undefined`.
- `judgeModified` reaches `:535` and returns `[]`.
- `whitespaceOnly` is false, and `carriesMalformedStringField` finds nothing.
- The committed file now parses to `value: 50`, and `checkRatchet` then evaluates live readings against that looser value.

The same trick hides a direction flip, using `"dir\u0065ction"`. It also works on a delete+add pair, because `reconstructLifecycle` and `judgeLifecycle` use the same regexes. Exploiting it takes a deliberate edit, and the guard exists to stop exactly that kind of edit (I5, ADR-0004 attack model).

**Fix:** rendered baselines never need escapes in key names. Fail closed whenever a ± or lifecycle line has an escape inside a key. `carriesMalformedStringField` already runs on both paths (`:611`, `:777`), so the check can go there.

<details>
<summary>Proposed fix</summary>

```diff
 const UNIT_RE = /"unit"\s*:\s*"((?:[^"\\]|\\.)*)"/g;
+// A property KEY containing any escape: JSON.parse decodes `"val\u0075e"`
+// to `value`, invisible to every literal-key regex above. Rendered
+// baselines never escape keys — fail closed.
+const ESCAPED_KEY_RE = /(?:^|[,{])\s*"(?:[^"\\]|\\.)*\\(?:[^"\\]|\\.)*"\s*:/;
```

```diff
 function carriesMalformedStringField(minus: string[], plus: string[], context: string[]): boolean {
+  for (const lines of [minus, plus, context]) {
+    if (lines.some((l) => ESCAPED_KEY_RE.test(l))) return true;
+  }
   const fields: Array<[RegExp, RegExp]> = [
```
</details>

Add named fixture tests for `"val\u0075e"` on the modified path and on the delete+add path, and for `"dir\u0065ction"`.
findings.title: Escaped JSON keys bypass every key regex and loosen the baseline unseen.

findings.body:
**Move `trustReviewRow` after the rows that skip contentless or voided reviews.**

In `REVIEW_ROWS`, `trustReviewRow` runs before `reviewDismissedRow`, `reviewAlreadyAnsweredRow`, and `approvalNoBodyRow`. For any review whose author is untrusted, `trustReviewRow` returns `blocked` with `untrusted_reviewer`, whatever the review state or body. When a trust policy is set, an author outside the trusted list is untrusted. A DISMISSED review, or an empty APPROVED, COMMENTED, or no-state review, from such an author therefore gets `blocked` instead of the `skip` that rows 9, 10, and 11 assign. The module contract says these reviews are not outstanding feedback.

`blocked` means a human must settle the item. The review loop records each blocked item as a `needs-human` reason, so a benign approval from an unlisted collaborator can stop the loop.

Moving the trust row after the skip rows keeps the trust gate ahead of the `actionable` fallback. Non-empty reviews from untrusted authors still reach `trustReviewRow` and still return `blocked`. The skipped reviews never reach a fixer, so no untrusted text is exposed.

<details>
<summary>♻️ Proposed reorder</summary>

```diff
 const REVIEW_ROWS: readonly RowFn<ReviewSummary>[] = [
   responderAuthoredReviewRow,
   botSkipReviewRow,
-  trustReviewRow,
   reviewDismissedRow,
   reviewAlreadyAnsweredRow,
   approvalNoBodyRow,
+  trustReviewRow,
 ];
```

</details>
findings.title: Move `trustReviewRow` after the rows that skip contentless or voided reviews.

findings.body:
**Treat a null author as non-automation.**

When `config.automationLogin` is `null`, `isAutomation` evaluates `authorLogin === config.automationLogin` as `null === null` for a comment with a null `authorLogin`, such as one from a deleted account. The thread and review skip rows (`src/ops/review/classifyThreads.ts:332-333` and `400-401`) run before their trust rows. A body that matches `skipPatterns` from a null author therefore returns `skip` (`bot_skip_notice`) instead of `blocked` (`untrusted_reviewer`). `isTrusted` already rejects null authors (line 224), and `isResponder` never matches them.

`ClassifyConfig.automationLogin` accepts `null` (`src/ops/review/classify.config.ts:102`). The review registry accepts it and forwards it unchanged (`src/ops/review/registry.ts:313` and `755`). A null value supplies no automation identity, so only a non-null login should be able to issue skip notices.

<details>
<summary>🛡️ Proposed fix</summary>

```diff
 const isAutomation = (authorLogin: string | null, config: ClassifyConfig): boolean =>
-  config.automationLogin === undefined || authorLogin === config.automationLogin;
+  config.automationLogin === undefined ||
+  (authorLogin !== null && authorLogin === config.automationLogin);
```

</details>
findings.title: Treat a null author as non-automation.
